subChunks.title: End-to-End Testing with Playwright
subChunks.hookHtml: Unit tests verify functions. Component tests verify components. End-to-end tests verify that a real user, in a real browser, can complete real tasks. Playwright is the modern E2E testing framework — it controls actual browsers (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit) with a powerful API that supports authentication flows, network interception, visual comparisons, and parallel cross-browser testing.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Playwright basics

// playwright.config.ts:
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './e2e',
  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:5173',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
    video: 'retain-on-failure',
  },
  projects: [
    { name: 'chromium', use: { browserName: 'chromium' } },
    { name: 'firefox',  use: { browserName: 'firefox' } },
    { name: 'webkit',   use: { browserName: 'webkit' } },
  ],
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run dev',
    url: 'http://localhost:5173',
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  },
});
// e2e/quest-board.spec.ts:
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('Quest Board', () => {
  test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/');
  });

  test('user can accept a quest', async ({ page }) => {
    // Navigate to quest board:
    await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Quests' }).click();

    // Find first quest and accept it:
    const firstQuest = page.getByTestId('quest-card').first();
    await firstQuest.getByRole('button', { name: 'Accept' }).click();

    // Verify it moved to the tracker:
    await expect(page.getByTestId('quest-tracker')).toContainText('Slay the Dragon');
  });
});

Authentication flows

// Authenticate once, reuse across tests:
// e2e/auth.setup.ts:
import { test as setup } from '@playwright/test';

setup('authenticate', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('admin@arcane.academy');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('test-password');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Log in' }).click();
  await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');

  // Save auth state to file:
  await page.context().storageState({ path: 'e2e/.auth/admin.json' });
});

// In test files — reuse saved auth:
// playwright.config.ts:
projects: [
  { name: 'setup', testMatch: /auth.setup.ts/ },
  {
    name: 'authenticated',
    use: { storageState: 'e2e/.auth/admin.json' },
    dependencies: ['setup'],
  },
]

Network interception

test('shows error state when API fails', async ({ page }) => {
  // Intercept the quest list API and return an error:
  await page.route('/api/quests', route => route.fulfill({
    status: 500,
    body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'Internal Server Error' }),
  }));

  await page.goto('/quests');

  // Verify the error state is displayed:
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Failed to load quests');
});

// Test loading state:
test('shows loading spinner during fetch', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('/api/quests', async route => {
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 2000)); // Slow response
    await route.continue();
  });

  await page.goto('/quests');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('loading-spinner')).toBeVisible();
});

Page Object Model

// e2e/pages/QuestBoardPage.ts:
export class QuestBoardPage {
  constructor(private page: Page) {}

  async goto() {
    await this.page.goto('/quests');
  }

  async acceptQuest(title: string) {
    const questCard = this.page.getByTestId('quest-card').filter({ hasText: title });
    await questCard.getByRole('button', { name: 'Accept' }).click();
  }

  async getTrackerQuests() {
    return this.page.getByTestId('tracker-item').allTextContents();
  }
}

// In tests — clean, readable:
test('accept quest flow', async ({ page }) => {
  const questBoard = new QuestBoardPage(page);
  await questBoard.goto();
  await questBoard.acceptQuest('Slay the Dragon');
  const tracker = await questBoard.getTrackerQuests();
  expect(tracker).toContain('Slay the Dragon');
});

Vex: "E2E tests are expensive — they're slow, brittle, and require a running application. Use them for your most critical user journeys: login, checkout, onboarding, the core workflow. Don't E2E test every button click — that's what component tests are for. A pyramid: many unit tests, some component tests, a few E2E tests for critical paths."

storyBeats.text: The new quest acceptance flow passes all unit tests. Then production breaks — a network condition the unit tests never simulated. A real browser test would have caught it.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: E2E tests run in a real browser. They click real buttons, fill real forms, navigate real routes. They test what unit and component tests can't: the integration of your entire stack. But they're slow and brittle — use them for your most critical paths and mock the network for edge cases.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Write Playwright tests for the quest board (architecture exercise — define the test structure):

  • Write a test for the happy path: navigate to quests, accept a quest, verify it appears in the tracker
  • Write a test for the error path: mock the API to return 500, verify error state is displayed
  • Write a Page Object Model class for the quest board with goto(), acceptQuest(), and getTrackerItems() methods
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Set up Playwright in your local quest board project and write a complete E2E test suite covering: (1) the full quest acceptance flow from the home page, (2) the member registration form with validation (fill invalid data, verify errors, fill valid data, verify redirect), (3) an authenticated admin flow using storageState to avoid re-logging in on every test. Run the tests in CI using a GitHub Actions workflow that starts the dev server and runs the full suite in parallel across Chromium and Firefox.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the testing pyramid — why should you have many unit tests, some component tests, and few E2E tests? What specific problems do E2E tests catch that unit and component tests miss? Walk through Playwright's authentication flow — why is storageState important for test performance? Explain network interception — what two categories of tests does it enable?

questions.prompt: Why is Playwright's `storageState` important for test suites that require authentication?
options: It saves browser cookies/localStorage after login so subsequent tests can start as authenticated users without repeating the login flow — making tests faster and more reliable
It stores test results between runs to avoid re-running passing tests
It persists page state so the browser doesn't restart between tests
It caches network responses to speed up tests
questions.answer: It saves browser cookies/localStorage after login so subsequent tests can start as authenticated users without repeating the login flow — making tests faster and more reliable
questions.explanation: If every test logs in, a 100-test suite runs the login UI flow 100 times — slow and brittle (if the login page changes, all tests fail). storageState runs login once in a setup project, saves the auth tokens to a file, and subsequent tests start with those tokens already in their browser context. Login happens once per test run regardless of how many authenticated tests exist.

questions.prompt: Which of these scenarios is best suited for E2E testing vs component testing?
options: E2E: complete checkout flow from cart to order confirmation. Component test: that the checkout button is disabled when the cart is empty.
E2E: that a button has the correct CSS class. Component test: the complete purchase flow.
E2E and component tests are equivalent — choose based on developer preference.
E2E: all button click handlers. Component test: multi-page navigation.
questions.answer: E2E: complete checkout flow from cart to order confirmation. Component test: that the checkout button is disabled when the cart is empty.
questions.explanation: E2E tests are expensive (slow, brittle, require a running server) so they should test integration across the whole stack — the complete journey a user takes through multiple pages, API calls, and state changes. The button disabled state is a single component concern — a component test is faster, more targeted, and more maintainable for this check.
